plan.topic_summary: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) refers to cryptographic algorithms designed to remain secure against attacks by quantum computers. For a 1–5 year investment view, the critical question is the pace and cost of migrating existing systems to PQC standards, the performance trade-offs in production environments, and the window during which 'harvest now, decrypt later' threats become material.
key_questions: What is the current status of NIST PQC standard finalization, and which major cloud and infrastructure providers have committed to specific PQC support timelines within the next 12 months?

What measurable performance overhead (latency, bandwidth, key size) do leading PQC algorithms introduce in production network and storage contexts, and how does this affect total cost of ownership for large-scale deployments?
What is the realistic enterprise and government migration timeline over the next 1–3 years, and what are the primary blockers (legacy systems, certificate infrastructure, interoperability)?
Will hybrid classical-plus-PQC schemes become the dominant deployment model over the 3–5 year horizon, or will pure PQC replace classical algorithms in most use cases?
What is the most credible near-term threat window for quantum computers capable of breaking widely deployed RSA and ECC, and how does that timeline interact with the migration schedule?

sources.title: A Survey of Post-Quantum Cryptography: Start of a New Race
sources.abstract: Information security is a fundamental and urgent issue in the digital transformation era. Cryptographic techniques and digital signatures have been applied to protect and authenticate relevant information. However, with the advent of quantum computers and quantum algorithms, classical cryptographic techniques have been in danger of collapsing because quantum computers can solve complex problems in polynomial time. Stemming from that risk, researchers worldwide have stepped up research on post-quantum algorithms to resist attack by quantum computers. In this review paper, we survey studies in recent years on post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and provide statistics on the number and content of publications, including a literature overview, detailed explanations of the most common methods so far, current implementation status, implementation comparisons, and discussion on future work. These studies focused on essential public cryptography techniques and digital signature schemes, and the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) launched a competition to select the best candidate for the expected standard. Recent studies have practically implemented the public key encryption/key encapsulation mechanism (PKE/KEM) and digital signature schemes on different hardware platforms and applied various optimization measures based on other criteria. Along with the increasing number of scientific publications, the recent trend of PQC research is increasingly evident and is the general trend in the cryptography industry. The movement opens up a promising avenue for researchers in public key cryptography and digital signatures, especially on algorithms selected by NIST.

sources.title: Energy Consumption of Post-Quantum Cryptography on Constrained and General-Purpose Architectures
sources.venue: Gillot, O., Buchanan, W. J., & Tehrani, M. G. (2026). Energy Consumption of Post-Quantum Cryptography on Constrained and General-Purpose Architectures. Cryptography, 10(4), 55
sources.abstract: With Q-day approaching, the transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) has begun, with governments across the US, UK and EU mandating migration to quantum-resistant standards. This paper benchmarks the three NIST-standardised PQC algorithms - FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) - across key generation, signing and verification operations, measuring both computational performance and energy consumption on a range of constrained IoT-class devices, from the 32-bit Raspberry Pi 1 and Zero to the 64-bit Raspberry Pi 4, as well as commodity laptop hardware. Using the FNIRSI FNB58 USB power meter and OpenSSL~3.5, results show that ML-KEM and ML-DSA achieve energy and speed efficiency comparable to classical elliptic-curve cryptography across all tested architectures. However, SLH-DSA signing is inadvisable on constrained hardware: energy costs for SLH-DSA signing on 32-bit devices were up to 243\% higher than on equivalent 64-bit hardware, making it impractical for resource-limited IoT deployments. These findings have direct implications for IoT security practitioners planning PQC migration.

sources.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography
sources.abstract: In this survey we propose to cover the prose of post-quantum cryptography over classical cryptography. We talk about the various cryptographic methods that are being practiced to safeguard our information. The future of secure communication is expected to be the implementation of quantum-safe cryptographic systems, and that in the post-quantum era, the development of post-quantum cryptography is essential for ensuring the security of sensitive data.

sources.title: Post Quantum Cryptography: A Review of Techniques, Challenges and Standardizations
sources.abstract: The development of large quantum computers will have dire consequences for cryptography. Most of the symmetric and asymmetric cryptographic algorithms are vulnerable to quantum algorithms. Grover’s search algorithm gives a square root time boost for the searching of the key in symmetric schemes like AES and 3DES. The security of asymmetric algorithms like RSA, Diffie Hellman, and ECC is based on the mathematical hardness of prime factorization and discrete logarithms. The best classical algorithms available take exponential time. Shor’s factoring algorithm can solve the problems in polynomial time. Major breakthroughs in quantum computing will render all the present-day widely used asymmetric cryptosystems insecure. This paper analyzes the vulnerability of the classical cryptosystems in the context of quantum computers, discusses various post-quantum cryptosystem families, discusses the status of the NIST post-quantum cryptography standardization process, provides a performance comparison of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms on different platforms, and finally provides a couple of future research directions in this field.

sources.title: A Comparative Performance Evaluation of Kyber, sntrup761, and FrodoKEM for Post-Quantum Cryptography
sources.abstract: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) aims to develop cryptographic algorithms that are secure against attacks from quantum computers. This paper compares the leading postquantum cryptographic algorithms, such as Kyber, sntrup761, and FrodoKEM, in terms of their security, performance, and real-world applicability. The review highlights the strengths and weaknesses of each algorithm and provides insights into future research directions. We also discuss the challenges of transitioning from classical to post-quantum systems and the potential impacts on various industries. This paper serves as a foundation for understanding the current state of post-quantum cryptography and its future prospects in the quantum computing era.

sources.title: A Survey on Post-Quantum Cryptography: State-of-the-Art and Challenges
sources.abstract: The paper explains that post-quantum cryptography is necessary due to the introduction of quantum computing causing certain algorithms to be broken. We analyze the different types of post-quantum cryptography, quantum cryptography and quantum-resistant cryptography, to provide a thorough understanding of the current solutions to the problems and their limitations. We explain the current state of quantum computing and how it has changed over time while discussing possible attacks on both types of post-quantum cryptography. Next, current post-quantum algorithms are discussed, and implementations are demonstrated. Lastly, we conclude that due to quantum cryptography's present limitations it is not a viable solution like it is often presented to be and that it is currently better to use quantum-resistant cryptography.

sources.title: Post-quantum cryptography and the quantum future of cybersecurity
sources.abstract: We review the current status of efforts to develop and deploy post-quantum cryptography on the Internet. Then we suggest specific ways in which quantum technologies might be used to enhance cybersecurity in the near future and beyond. We focus on two goals: protecting the secret keys that are used in classical cryptography, and ensuring the trustworthiness of quantum computations. These goals may soon be within reach, thanks to recent progress in both theory and experiment. This progress includes interactive protocols for testing quantumness as well as for performing uncloneable cryptographic computations; and experimental demonstrations of device-independent random number generators, device-independent quantum key distribution, quantum memories, and analog quantum simulators.

sources.title: The Mathematical Foundation of Post-Quantum Cryptography
sources.abstract: On July 5, 2022, the National Institute of Standards and Technology announced four possible post-quantum cryptography standards, three of them are based on lattice theory and the other one is based on Hash function. It is well-known that the security of the lattice cryptography relies on the hardness of the shortest vector problem (SVP) and the closest vector problem (CVP). In fact, the SVP is a sphere packing problem and the CVP is a sphere covering problem. Furthermore, both SVP and CVP are equivalent to arithmetic problems of positive definite quadratic forms. This paper will briefly introduce the post-quantum cryptography and show its connections with sphere packing, sphere covering, and positive definite quadratic forms.

sources.title: Applications of Post-Quantum Cryptography
sources.venue: European Conference on Cyber Warfare and Security
sources.abstract: With the constantly advancing capabilities of quantum computers, conventional cryptographic systems relying on complex math problems may encounter unforeseen vulnerabilities. Unlike regular computers, which are often deemed cost-ineffective in cryptographic attacks, quantum computers have a significant advantage in calculation speed. This distinction potentially makes currently used algorithms less secure or even completely vulnerable, compelling the exploration of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) as the most reasonable solution to quantum threats. This review aims to provide current information on applications, benefits, and challenges associated with the PQC. The review employs a systematic scoping review with the scope restricted to the years 2022 and 2023; only articles that were published in scientific journals were used in this paper. The review examined the articles on the applications of quantum computing in various spheres. However, the scope of this paper was restricted to the domain of the PQC because most of the analyzed articles featured this field. Subsequently, the paper is analyzing various PQC algorithms, including lattice-based, hash-based, code-based, multivariate polynomial, and isogeny-based cryptography. Each algorithm is being judged based on its potential applications, robustness, and challenges. All the analyzed algorithms are promising for the post-quantum era in such applications as digital signatures, communication channels, and IoT. Moreover, some of the algorithms are already implemented in the spheres of banking transactions, communication, and intellectual property. Meanwhile, despite their potential, these algorithms face serious challenges since they lack standardization, require vast amounts of storage and computation power, and might have unknown vulnerabilities that can be discovered only with years of cryptanalysis. This overview aims to give a basic understanding of the current state of post-quantum cryptography with its applications and challenges. As the world enters the quantum era, this review not only shows the need for strong security methods that can resist quantum attacks but also presents an optimistic outlook on the future of secure communications, guided by advancements in quantum technology. By bridging the gap between theoretical research and practical implementation, this paper aims to inspire further innovation and collaboration in the field.

sources.title: Obfuscated Quantum and Post-Quantum Cryptography
sources.venue: IEEE International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC) 2026 Kobe, Japan
sources.abstract: In this work, we present an experimental deployment of a new design for combined quantum key distribution (QKD) and post-quantum cryptography (PQC). Novel to our system is the dynamic obfuscation of the QKD-PQC sequence of operations, the number of operations, and parameters related to the operations; coupled to the integration of a GPS-free quantum synchronization protocol within the QKD process. We compare the performance and overhead of our QKD-PQC system relative to a standard QKD system with one-time pad encryption, demonstrating that our design can operate in real time with little additional overhead caused by the new security features. Since our system can offer additional defensive strategies against a wide spectrum of practical attacks that undermine deployed QKD, PQC, and certain combinations of these two primitives, we suggest that our design represents one of the most secure communication systems currently available. Given the dynamic nature of its obfuscation attributes, our new system can also be adapted in the field to defeat yet-to-be-discovered practical attacks.

sources.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Neural Network
sources.abstract: In recent years, quantum computers and Shor quantum algorithm have posed a threat to current mainstream asymmetric cryptography methods (e.g. RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC)). Therefore, it is necessary to construct a Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) method to resist quantum computing attacks. Therefore, this study proposes a PQC-based neural network that maps a code-based PQC method to a neural network structure and enhances the security of ciphertexts with non-linear activation functions, random perturbation of ciphertexts, and uniform distribution of ciphertexts. In practical experiments, this study uses cellular network signals as a case study to demonstrate that encryption and decryption can be performed by the proposed PQC-based neural network with the uniform distribution of ciphertexts. In the future, the proposed PQC-based neural network could be applied to various applications.

sources.title: PQCMC: Post-Quantum Cryptography McEliece-Chen Implicit Certificate Scheme
sources.abstract: In recent years, the elliptic curve Qu-Vanstone (ECQV) implicit certificate scheme has found application in security credential management systems (SCMS) and secure vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication to issue pseudonymous certificates. However, the vulnerability of elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC) to polynomial-time attacks posed by quantum computing raises concerns. In order to enhance resistance against quantum computing threats, various post-quantum cryptography methods have been adopted as standard (e.g. Dilithium) or candidate standard methods (e.g. McEliece cryptography), but state of the art has proven to be challenging to implement implicit certificates using lattice-based cryptography methods. Therefore, this study proposes a post-quantum cryptography McEliece-Chen (PQCMC) based on an efficient random invertible matrix generation method to issue pseudonymous certificates with less computation time. The study provides mathematical models to validate the key expansion process for implicit certificates. Furthermore, comprehensive security evaluations and discussions are conducted to demonstrate that distinct implicit certificates can be linked to the same end entity. In experiments, a comparison is conducted between the certificate length and computation time to evaluate the performance of the proposed PQCMC. This study demonstrates the viability of the implicit certificate scheme based on PQC as a means of countering quantum computing threats.

sources.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Anonymous Scheme -- PQCWC: Post-Quantum Cryptography Winternitz-Chen
sources.abstract: As quantum computing technology matures, it poses a threat to the security of mainstream asymmetric cryptographic methods. In response, the National Institute of Standards and Technology released the final version of post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) algorithm standards in August 2024. These post-quantum cryptographic algorithms are primarily based on lattice-based and hash-based cryptography. Therefore, this study proposes the Post-Quantum Cryptography Winternitz-Chen (PQCWC) anonymous scheme, aimed at exploring the design of anonymous schemes based on PQC for future applications in privacy protection. The anonymous scheme designed in this study is mainly built on the Winternitz signature scheme, which can prevent the original public key from being exposed in the certificate. Furthermore, the PQCWC anonymous scheme integrates the butterfly key expansion mechanism, proposing the first hash-based butterfly key expansion mechanism in the world, achieving anonymity for both the registration authority and the certificate authority, thereby fully protecting privacy. In the experimental environment, this study compares various hash algorithms, including Secure Hash Algorithm-1 (SHA-1), the SHA-2 series, the SHA-3 series, and the BLAKE series. The results demonstrate that the proposed anonymous scheme can achieve anonymity without increasing key length, signature length, key generation time, signature generation time, or signature verification time.

sources.title: Exploring Post-Quantum Cryptography: Review and Directions for the Transition Process
sources.abstract: As quantum computing advances, current cryptographic protocols are increasingly vulnerable to quantum attacks, particularly those based on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) like RSA or Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC). This paper presents a comprehensive review of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) as a solution to protect digital systems in the quantum era. We provide an in-depth analysis of various quantum-resistant cryptographic algorithms, including lattice-based, code-based, hash-based, isogeny-based, and multivariate approaches. The review highlights the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) PQC standardization process, highlighting key algorithms, such as CRYSTALS–Kyber, CRYSTALS–Dilithium, Falcon, and SPHINCS+, and discusses the strengths, vulnerabilities, and implementation challenges of the leading algorithms. In addition, we explore transition strategies for organizations, emphasizing hybrid cryptography to ensure backward compatibility during migration. This study offers key insights into the future of cryptographic standards and the critical steps necessary to prepare for the transition from classical to quantum-resistant systems.

sources.title: On Post-Quantum Cryptography Authentication for Quantum Key Distribution
sources.abstract: The traditional way for a Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) user to join a quantum network is by authenticating themselves using pre-shared key material. While this approach is sufficient for small-scale networks, it becomes impractical as the network grows, due to the total quadratic increase in the number of pre-shared keys required. To address this scalability issue, Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) combined with Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) offers a more scalable solution, allowing users to authenticate the QKD traffic remotely to obtain information-theoretical secure (ITS) keys under the presented assumptions. Unlike traditional PKI, which relies on classical cryptographic algorithms such as RSA, the approach presented in this paper leverages PQC algorithms that are believed to be resistant to quantum attacks. Similarly to the SIGMA or TLS protocols, authentication, confidentiality, and integrity are achievable against bounded adversaries to ensure secure and scalable quantum networks.

sources.title: Secure Computation After Quantum: PQC, Confidential Clouds, and Policy-Grade Auditability
sources.venue: International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)
sources.abstract: Abstract: This study investigates how secure computation can remain trustworthy during the post-quantum transition, in which large-scale quantum computation threatens the public-key primitives used for key exchange, authentication, and software trust. The analysis treats quantum readiness as a systems property rather than a cryptographic substitution exercise. In practical deployments, cryptographic migrations change protocol sizes and performance characteristics, while cloud execution substrates introduce privileged attack surfaces that can expose data despite formally strong cryptography. A unified architecture is proposed that couples standardised post-quantum cryptography (PQC) for key establishment and digital signatures with confidential cloud execution (hardware-backed isolation and remote attestation) and with policy-grade auditability implemented via policy-as-code plus cryptographic provenance. The evaluation uses real, published parameter sizes from standardised PQC algorithms and real published performance measurements for trusted execution environments to quantify bandwidth overhead, handshake expansion, and the capacity impact of protected execution. The results show that PQC adoption can introduce substantial protocol-layer size expansion, with digital signature payloads frequently dominating bandwidth budgets relative to key encapsulation. Hybrid deployment profiles increase overhead further because classical and post-quantum materials are transmitted together, supporting staged rollouts with explicit deprecation timelines. Confidential computing reduces exposure to compromised hypervisors but imposes workload-sensitive overheads, motivating selective isolation of high-value computations combined with continuous, evidence-centric governance. Keywords post-quantum cryptography; confidential computing; trusted execution environments; policy-as-code; auditability; attestation; cryptographic agility; compliance; secure computation; zero trust.

sources.title: A Novel Masking Scheme with Low Additional Overhead for LWE-Based PQC Family
PDRL-PQCS: Proactive Deep Reinforcement Learning for Real-Time PQC Configuration in ITS with Edge Collaboration
sources.abstract: The emergence of quantum computing presents significant challenges for intelligent transportation systems (ITS), which rely on traditional public-key cryptography, demanding both strong security and low-latency operation. This highlights an urgent requirement for post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) algorithms to guarantee long-term protection. However, a direct integration of PQC into ITS may introduce latency and inefficiency, as static implementations cannot adapt to dynamic traffic conditions and may apply excessive security in low-risk contexts, resulting in unnecessary computational overhead, particularly within resource-constrained edge computing environments. To mitigate these issues, the PDRL-PQCS (Predictive Deep Reinforcement Learning for Post-Quantum Cryptography Selection) framework is proposed. This approach employs a Transformer-based module to generate multi-step predictions of traffic flow and computational load, thereby providing proactive contextual awareness. These predictions subsequently inform a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agent, which dynamically selects optimal parameter configurations for the CRYSTALS-Kyber PQC algorithm in real time, enabling adaptive security-performance balancing across the heterogeneous nodes of an ITS edge computing network. Through this two-stage approach, PDRL-PQCS adapts PQC parameters within defined security bounds to optimally balance security assurance with operational efficiency. An extensive experimental evaluation assesses the framework under three representative traffic scenarios with diverse resource availability and congestion levels. Results indicate that PDRL-PQCS achieves 10%–20% higher overall performance compared to baseline methods across various challenging conditions.

sources.title: PQC Protection for AI Workloads - A Performance-Aware Migration Framework
sources.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence workloads have become deeply woven into healthcare, finance, defense, and critical infrastructure, and the encryption protecting those workloads now sits under a clock. A sufficiently capable quantum computer running Shor's algorithm will break the asymmetric cryptography - RSA, Elliptic Curve Cryptography, and Diffie-Hellman - that guard data in transit and the roots of trust behind device and model authentication. The threat is not confined to some distant future either. Adversaries are already intercepting and storing encrypted traffic under a “harvest now, decrypt later” strategy, betting that quantum hardware will catch up before the data loses its value. This paper studies what actually happens when we move AI workloads onto the post-quantum algorithms that the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) finalized in 2024, namely ML-KEM for key establishment and ML-DSA for digital signatures. We frame the problem specifically for heterogeneous compute platforms - the mix of general-purpose cores, GPU accelerators, embedded controllers, and system-on-chip (SoC) endpoints on which modern AI is deployed - because these environments carry latency budgets, memory ceilings, and signature-size constraints that generic cryptographic benchmarks tend to ignore. Using a controlled experimental design that compares a classical baseline, a pure post-quantum configuration, and a hybrid configuration across transformer inference, distributed training, and federated learning, we characterize the overhead these algorithms introduce and where it concentrates. We then translate those measurements into a practical, phased migration framework that maps workload classes to cryptographic strategies and sequences the transition to preserve operational continuity. The central finding is that post-quantum protection for AI is far less a raw performance problem than an engineering and governance problem: symmetric encryption already survives quantum attack, key exchange migrates with negligible cost, and the real difficulty lies in the larger signatures and longer-lived roots of trust that authentication depends on. The proposed framework gives engineering leaders a concrete way to prioritize, sequence, and verify the migration on the heterogeneous platforms where AI actually runs.

sources.title: Practical hybrid PQC-QKD protocols with enhanced security and performance
sources.abstract: Quantum resistance is vital for emerging cryptographic systems as quantum technologies continue to advance towards large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers. Resistance may be offered by quantum key distribution (QKD), which provides information-theoretic security using quantum states of photons, but may be limited by transmission loss at long distances. An alternative approach uses classical means and is conjectured to be resistant to quantum attacks, so-called post-quantum cryptography (PQC), but it is yet to be rigorously proven, and its current implementations are computationally expensive. To overcome the security and performance challenges present in each, here we develop hybrid protocols by which QKD and PQC inter-operate within a joint quantum-classical network. In particular, we consider different hybrid designs that may offer enhanced speed and/or security over the individual performance of either approach. Furthermore, we present a method for analyzing the security of hybrid protocols in key distribution networks. Our hybrid approach paves the way for joint quantum-classical communication networks, which leverage the advantages of both QKD and PQC and can be tailored to the requirements of various practical networks.

sources.title: Exploration of PQC-Based Digital Signature Schemes in TLS Certificates
sources.venue: The Asian Bulletin of Big Data Management
sources.abstract: The rapid development in quantum computers brings huge risks to traditional cryptographic systems. This paper talks about the integration of PQC-based digital signature schemes to solve challenges posed on Transport Layer Security certificates. In this paper, we give an analysis of the efficacy, security, and performance implications of various schemes in PQC—particularly lattice-based, hash-based, and multivariate polynomial-based algorithms. We detail more closely the challenges of the real deployment, directly connected with these digital signatures, considering communication overhead and computational costs. Our findings indicate that hybrid certificate chains, which integrate multiple PQC schemes, offer a feasible solution for a seamless transition to quantum-resistant standards with manageable performance trade-offs. Moreover, our study extends to the quantification of security benefits these PQC schemes provide against both quantum and classical computational attacks, underscoring their potential in enhancing the resilience of digital communication systems. This paper aims to contribute valuable insights to ongoing standardization discussions and support the broader adoption of PQC, thereby ensuring robust and future-proof security in digital communications amidst the advancing quantum computing era.

sources.title: Operationalising Post Quantum TLS Automated Configuration Profiling and Hybrid PQC Deployment in Financial Infrastructure
sources.abstract: Organisations are upgrading their cryptographic infrastructure to become quantum safe before large scale quantum computers materialise. Post quantum cryptography (PQC) standards now exist for key exchange and digital signatures, but the urgent question for adopters is how to operationalise PQC in complex environments with confidence. In banking, Transport Layer Security (TLS), for example, protects data in transit across public facing channels and internal services, and is terminated at many heterogeneous endpoints (web servers, API gateways, load balancers, reverse proxies), each a potential quantum vulnerable component and migration target. We argue that the bottleneck is operational rather than algorithmic, hybrid key exchanges such as MLKEM and hybrid MLKEM key exchanges are already available in mainstream libraries, but security teams lack precise visibility into TLS configurations and repeatable methods for enabling PQC compatible settings across a heterogeneous estate. This paper presents a configuration parsing methodology that automatically extracts and normalises TLS cryptographic posture across dominant enterprise web server stacks, producing a unified, provenance traced cryptographic inventory as a foundation for migration and compliance. We demonstrate the approach on 8,443 real world Nginx configurations from public repositories and in a proof of concept deployment at a financial institution, where MLKEM and hybrid MLKEM key exchanges at TLS termination points (web server and API gateway) securing an internal application, with zero application layer changes and manageable performance overhead.

sources.title: SoK: PQC PAKEs Design, Security and Performance
sources.abstract: Password Authenticated Key Exchange (PAKE) establishes secure communication channels using passwords for authentication. Currently, standardized PAKEs rely on classical asymmetric cryptography. However, these PAKEs may become insecure should the expected quantum threat become a reality. Despite the growing interest in realizing quantum-safe PAKEs, they did not receive much attention from the ongoing Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) integration efforts. Hence, there is a significant awareness gap compared to PQC primitives subject to the official standardization processes. We provide a comprehensive overview of existing PQC PAKEs, classify their design rationales and authentication methods, and address aspects related to their security and performance. We identify PAKE designs that are still unexplored in the PQC realm and discuss the possibility of their adaptation. Thus, we offer a detailed reference for future work on PQC PAKEs.

sources.title: Integrating PQC into standard industry protocols
sources.venue: Brno University of Technology Digital Library (Brno University of Technology)
sources.abstract: Tato diplomová práce se zabývá možnostmi integrace postkvantové kryptografie do pro- tokolů a systémů využívaných v průmyslovém prostředí a v prostředí infrastruktury veřej- ných klíčů. V teoretické části jsou popsány systémy infrastruktury veřejných klíčů, certi- fikáty standardu X.509 a moderní kryptografické algoritmy včetně postkvantové krypto- grafie. Dále jsou analyzovány protokoly EST, SCEP, LoRaWAN a ACME, u nichž byly identifikovány kryptografické mechanismy a možnosti jejich nahrazení za kvantově odolné varianty. S ohledem na infrastrukturu veřejných klíčů pak byly prozkoumány některé ve- řejně dostupné systémy pro management PKI a z nich byl vybrán systém LamassuIoT pro integraci postkvantové ochrany do jeho mechanismů distribuce certifikátů. Implementace byla zaměřena na proces distribuce certifikátů pomocí protokolu EST v systému Lamas- suIoT. Systém byl rozšířen o podporu podpisového schématu ML-DSA a komunikační proces protokolu EST byl převeden na hybridní výměnu klíče ML-KEM-768+X25519. Funkčnost byla ověřena pomocí klientské sady na STM32. Výsledná konfigurace byla změřena a naměřené hodnoty ukazují dopad kvantově odolných kryptografických algo- ritmů na provozní vlastnosti systému. Naměřené hodnoty byly srovnány s teoretickým odhadem založeným na údajích uvedených v oficiálních specifikacích algoritmů. Měření dopadu na výkon bylo provedeno, ale jeho výsledky neprokázaly zásadní zvýšení výpočetní náročnosti na straně serveru.

sources.title: On the Security Implications of PQC in TLS: Handshake Exhaustion and IDS Degradation
sources.abstract: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is increasingly being integrated into TLS 1.3 to enhance resilience against quantum-enabled attacks. However, the additional computational and communication overhead introduced by PQC primitives during the handshake phase may also amplify the impact of TLS handshake exhaustion attacks, leading to more severe Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) threats. In this study, we establish an empirical testbed consisting of one PQC-enabled TLS server and ten attacking nodes, generating over 16.5 GB of mixed traffic data that includes both legitimate browsing behavior and high-intensity handshake exhaustion attacks. Experimental results show that PQC-TLS can prolong periods of sustained high CPU utilization on the server by up to 88 times, significantly amplifying the effectiveness of such attacks. Furthermore, we evaluate state-of-the-art deep learning-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) and observe a substantial decline in attack detection performance under PQC traffic conditions. In particular, exosphere achieves only around 50% recall, while HyperVision's AU-ROC degrades to near-random levels (0.49), revealing critical detection blind spots in existing IDS when operating in PQC environments. The main contributions of this work are threefold: (1) we systematically quantify and analyze the root causes of IDS detection blind spots in PQC settings; (2) we publicly release a comprehensive PQC-DDoS hybrid traffic dataset, including precise attack timestamps and server-side resource monitoring data; and (3) we open-source all experimental code and AWS deployment scripts, enabling a fully reproducible cloud-based testing environment. These resources aim to support both academia and industry in developing next-generation PQC-aware intrusion detection systems.

sources.title: Navigating the NIST PQC Standards: Trade-offs and Case Studies
sources.abstract: The rapid advancement of quantum computing poses a significant threat to classical cryptographic systems, particularly to widely used public-key schemes that rely on integer factorisation and the discrete logarithm problem. To ensure long-term data security against potential quantum adversaries, post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is currently standardised by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). This paper goes beyond a theoretical overview by employing a systematic methodology to evaluate the empirical performance trade-offs of the newly standardised algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA) and key finalists (FN-DSA and HQC). Based on a comprehensive review of fragmented performance data, the work presents a comparative analysis focusing on data overhead, computational latency, and resource efficiency. As a primary contribution, this study proposes a deployment-oriented taxonomy that explicitly maps these PQC standards to optimal practical use cases, considering diverse constraints across Internet of Things, cloud environments, and blockchain networks. Furthermore, the paper addresses critical real-world deployment challenges, such as vulnerabilities to side-channel attacks and hardware-level implementation constraints. Ultimately, this work systematises current knowledge into a unified decision-making framework, guiding system architects in complex migration towards a quantum-resilient digital ecosystem.

sources.title: NoisePQC++: A Unified NIST-Compliant PQC and Hybrid-PQC Implementation of the Noise Protocol
sources.abstract: The threat of quantum computers to classical public-key cryptography has created an urgent need to evolve secure communication protocols with post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) primitives. The Noise Protocol Framework, widely used in systems such as WireGuard and WhatsApp, traditionally relies on the Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) public-key exchange scheme, which is vulnerable to quantum threats. In this paper, we present NoisePQC++, a unified C++23 implementation of the Noise Protocol framework augmented with post-quantum Key Encapsulation Mechanisms and Hybrid Forward Secrecy. Our design integrates the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) standardized ML-KEM algorithm alongside classical ECDH, enabling full PQC, hybrid ECDH+PQC handshakes, and unified support for all 57 classical Noise handshake pattern variants, 13 post-quantum Noise handshakes, and their hybrid variants. Compared with prior work, NoisePQC++ offers broader protocol coverage, more complete implementation support, and greater flexibility. Our evaluation shows minimal overhead under normal network conditions and acceptable overhead in adverse cases, while significantly improving resistance against quantum adversaries. These results indicate that NIST-standardized post-quantum and hybrid Noise handshakes are practical and provide a credible basis for future deployment.

findings.claim: PQC raises bandwidth and handshake sizes, and signatures rather than key exchange dominate the cost. Hybrid classical+PQC deployments add more overhead because both sets of material are sent.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The size figures come from published parameter sizes, not new field measurements. A second paper (src_360d24bdaa) says hybrid certificate chains have 'manageable' trade-offs, so the severity of the penalty is contested. Both are abstract-only and appear in lower-profile venues.
findings.supporting_excerpt: The results show that PQC adoption can introduce substantial protocol-layer size expansion, with digital signature payloads frequently dominating bandwidth budgets relative to key encapsulation.

findings.claim: PQC-enabled TLS may widen the denial-of-service attack surface. In one testbed, handshake-exhaustion attacks kept server CPU high far longer, and deep-learning intrusion detection lost much of its accuracy on PQC traffic.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is an arXiv preprint and not peer reviewed. The testbed is small (one server, ten attacking nodes), so it may not generalise to production load balancers, hardware offload or rate limiting. The IDS result may reflect models trained on classical traffic rather than a fundamental flaw. No independent replication appears in the set.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Experimental results show that PQC-TLS can prolong periods of sustained high CPU utilization on the server by up to 88 times, significantly amplifying the effectiveness of such attacks.

findings.claim: The evidence on PQC performance cost conflicts. Some studies report large overheads (bandwidth expansion, CPU amplification under attack, latency in edge systems). Others report minimal or non-significant overhead (a Noise-protocol implementation, an EST/PKI proof of concept on STM32). Results depend heavily on workload, platform and what is measured.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The 'low overhead' claims (src_93fbebde13, a preprint; src_971eca27d6, a thesis whose abstract says server-side computational cost did not rise substantially) concern normal conditions or the server side. The 'high overhead' claims concern adversarial load, bandwidth or constrained edge nodes. No common benchmark makes these results comparable, and all are abstract-only.

findings.claim: The security of PQC rests on conjecture, not proof. The cited paper describes PQC as not yet rigorously proven and its current implementations as computationally expensive. This is a residual cryptanalytic and maturity risk, and one reason hybrid or QKD-combined designs are proposed.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a single arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed, and its authors have an interest in promoting hybrid PQC-QKD. It is a general statement of the state of knowledge, not evidence of a specific break. QKD carries its own distance and loss limits, so the alternative is not risk-free.
findings.supporting_excerpt: An alternative approach uses classical means and is conjectured to be resistant to quantum attacks, so-called post-quantum cryptography (PQC), but it is yet to be rigorously proven

findings.claim: Implementation-level risks, namely side-channel leakage and hardware constraints, remain open deployment problems for the new standards. Countermeasures such as masking for lattice-based schemes are still an active research topic.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: src_10a7c54025 is a review built on 'fragmented performance data', so it adds no new measurements. src_85fc0e903a has metadata only (no abstract), so its title is the only evidence. Whether masking overhead is a practical barrier is not shown in the set; this is a gap.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Furthermore, the paper addresses critical real-world deployment challenges, such as vulnerabilities to side-channel attacks and hardware-level implementation constraints.

findings.claim: The migration bottleneck may be operational (cryptographic inventory, configuration visibility, heterogeneous endpoints) rather than algorithmic. Legacy and industrial protocols (EST, SCEP, LoRaWAN, ACME) also need case-by-case adaptation, and password-authenticated key exchange gets little attention in current PQC integration work.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Three independent sources point to migration friction beyond the core algorithms. src_8b5ec17baf is a preprint; its 8,443 configurations come from public repositories and may not represent enterprise estates, and it has one financial-institution proof of concept. src_971eca27d6 is a master's thesis. src_45a730fcff is a survey that identifies an awareness gap.
findings.supporting_excerpt: security teams lack precise visibility into TLS configurations and repeatable methods for enabling PQC compatible settings across a heterogeneous estate.

findings.claim: Resource-constrained and heterogeneous platforms (edge nodes, embedded controllers, SoCs, AI accelerators) face latency, memory and signature-size constraints that generic PQC benchmarks may not capture. Adaptive or AI-driven mitigations add complexity and have not been shown to be robust.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Both abstracts are truncated, so the quantitative results are not visible. src_9987e02f40 is a non-peer-reviewed Research Square preprint. The ITS paper evaluates its own DRL selector, likely in simulation or controlled experiments; the abstract does not say. An adaptive scheme that lowers parameters in 'low-risk contexts' could itself weaken security margins. This is my inference, not a stated result.
findings.supporting_excerpt: However, a direct integration of PQC into ITS may introduce latency and inefficiency, as static implementations cannot adapt to dynamic traffic conditions

findings.claim: None of the retrieved papers gives evidence on when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer will exist. The urgency framing ('harvest now, decrypt later') is therefore an assumption inherited from outside the evidence set, not something these papers test.
findings.label: assumption
findings.rationale: The abstracts use conditional language ('sufficiently capable quantum computer', 'before large scale quantum computers materialise'). This is a gap in the search coverage, not a finding that the threat is unreal. The urgency claim should be checked against quantum-hardware and resource-estimation literature, which is absent here.

hype_flags: 'Future-proof' / 'quantum-safe' framing: PQC security is conjectured, not proven, and implementations are still being hardened against side-channels.
'Minimal overhead' / 'practical' claims from single-implementation preprints (e.g. Noise protocol): these cover normal conditions, not adversarial load or constrained devices.
Harvest-now-decrypt-later urgency is asserted without any timeline evidence in this set.
AI/deep-reinforcement-learning-based PQC parameter selection: novelty framing with unclear real-world validation, since abstracts are truncated.
Hybrid certificate chains described as 'manageable' trade-offs, while another paper in the set finds hybrid profiles increase overhead.
Confidential-cloud plus PQC 'unified architecture' claims rest on combining published parameters and measurements, not end-to-end deployments.

finding.claim: S1 is labelled verified_fact/high, but the cited abstract only supports the 2022 count (three lattice, one hash-based). "Establishing lattices as the dominant design family" is the agent's inference. The framing is also dated: src_d4018cdf1e reports final standards in August 2024, and src_10a7c54025 lists finalists beyond lattices and hashes. The finding omits that the standard set is being diversified (a code-based finalist, HQC, is named), so lattice dominance is not settled.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The count of lattice versus hash algorithms is stated in src_4aefcdcced. The "dominant family" conclusion and its "high" confidence go beyond that. The abstracts do not discuss the code-based finalist's role, so that point rests on the listing in src_10a7c54025 alone.
finding.supporting_excerpt: the National Institute of Standards and Technology released the final version of post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) algorithm standards in August 2024

finding.claim: S3 generalises the energy and speed parity with elliptic-curve cryptography beyond what one abstract-only preprint shows. The tests used Raspberry Pi boards and a laptop, with no microcontroller-class devices and no radio or bandwidth energy. Compute and energy parity does not address the bandwidth and handshake-size expansion, or the denial-of-service amplification, reported by other papers in the evidence set.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The finding is one study measured in one way. src_36248af4c5 reports substantial protocol size expansion and src_ae754525d8 reports up to 88 times longer high CPU under handshake exhaustion. Together they show that per-operation parity does not mean system-level parity. The finding should be scoped to per-operation compute and energy on these boards.
finding.supporting_excerpt: measuring both computational performance and energy consumption on a range of constrained IoT-class devices, from the 32-bit Raspberry Pi 1 and Zero to the 64-bit Raspberry Pi 4, as well as commodity laptop hardware

finding.claim: S4 is labelled unverified_claim/low, yet the abstract states the SLH-DSA result explicitly, so the label understates the support. The 243% figure compares 32-bit boards (Pi 1/Zero) with a different, newer 64-bit board (Pi 4). That confounds architecture with CPU generation, and it is not a comparison against classical signatures. The finding's absolute "inadvisable" omits that it applies to signing only and that the paper's wording is "constrained hardware".
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The label does not match the evidence: the abstract does support the claim. The substantive weakness is the confounded comparison and the single preprint. The abstract says nothing about use cases, such as verify-only devices, where SLH-DSA signing cost would not matter.
finding.supporting_excerpt: energy costs for SLH-DSA signing on 32-bit devices were up to 243\% higher than on equivalent 64-bit hardware

finding.claim: S5 presents hybrid cryptography as the transition recommendation without its costs. Papers in the evidence set report that hybrid profiles add bandwidth and handshake overhead because both classical and post-quantum material is sent. Hybrids also add complexity, and the cited review is abstract-only, so how strongly it recommends hybrids is unknown.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt from src_36248af4c5 shows the trade-off that S5 leaves out. Backward compatibility is a benefit, but the finding should state the overhead cost alongside it.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Hybrid deployment profiles increase overhead further because classical and post-quantum materials are transmitted together
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S6 is correct as a conditional statement but drops the condition. The vulnerability depends on large quantum computers that do not yet exist, and no retrieved paper estimates when they might. Also, src_5625041338, one of the three cited sources, does not mention Shor's algorithm or RSA/ECC in its abstract, so it does not support this specific claim. src_5fbbdb1b17 names only Shor's factoring algorithm, so extending it to discrete-log problems (DH, ECC) is not shown in its abstract.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The "verified_fact/high" label fits the factoring statement but not the unconditional wording or the citation breadth. This complements R8 on the missing timeline.
finding.supporting_excerpt: The development of large quantum computers will have dire consequences for cryptography.

finding.claim: S7 reports an argument from a single arXiv survey preprint that PQC is "currently the more viable solution" than quantum cryptography. It is presented as an established finding. Other retrieved papers treat PQC and QKD as complementary and propose hybrid designs, which suggests the question is contested. The two address different problems and have different assumptions.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The finding correctly reports what the survey argues, but the authors' stance is not independent evidence. src_6a33060056 and src_2a1b2216b3 see value in combining or complementing PQC with quantum techniques. It should be labelled as one survey's position, not a settled comparison.
finding.supporting_excerpt: due to quantum cryptography's present limitations it is not a viable solution like it is often presented to be

finding.claim: S8 presents PQC-based PKI as a scalable authentication fix for QKD networks without noting its security cost. Authentication then relies on computational assumptions against bounded adversaries. That weakens the information-theoretic framing that motivates QKD, and the keys are described as information-theoretically secure only "under the presented assumptions". The source is a single preprint proposal, not a deployment result.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The scalability benefit is real in the abstract, but the quoted limitation to bounded adversaries is an important caveat. The finding should note that PQC authentication introduces a computational-security dependency into QKD.
finding.supporting_excerpt: authentication, confidentiality, and integrity are achievable against bounded adversaries to ensure secure and scalable quantum networks.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S10, S11 and S12 rest on author-reported results from what appear to be closely related arXiv preprints (PQCMC, PQCWC, PQC neural network). They cannot be treated as independent corroboration and are not NIST-standardised. The claims ("proven challenging" for lattice implicit certificates; no increase in key, signature or timing cost; increased ciphertext security from a neural mapping) are self-assessed. The neural-network abstract shows only that encryption and decryption work with uniformly distributed ciphertexts, with no cryptanalysis, so "increase ciphertext security" is unsupported.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Labelling these verified_fact conflates what the papers claim with what has been validated. The abstracts show no external review, no security reductions for the neural construction, and no comparison against standardised schemes. The shared title pattern points to a single research line, which is an inference from titles only.
finding.supporting_excerpt: encryption and decryption can be performed by the proposed PQC-based neural network with the uniform distribution of ciphertexts

finding.claim: S13's claimed shift from algorithm and survey work toward deployment concerns is a trend claim made from a small, retrieval-selected sample of abstracts. It has no time-series or bibliometric basis. Several cited sources are themselves reviews. One cited source, src_6a440a8da3, has an abstract that is only a NIST boilerplate disclaimer with no content, so it cannot support any thematic claim.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt from src_6a440a8da3 shows the abstract carries no substantive content on migration or deployment. A shift over time would need papers sampled across years, and this evidence set was assembled by topical search. The 'shift' should be softened to 'deployment themes are prominent in the retrieved papers'.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Certain equipment, instruments, software, or materials, commercial or non-commercial, are identified in this paper in order to specify the experimental procedure adequately.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

limitations: Only 12 papers were available, and I saw abstracts only, some truncated (src_9987e02f40, src_5c4c39a5eb, src_8b5ec17baf, src_ae754525d8) and one with no abstract (src_85fc0e903a).
Several sources are arXiv or Research Square preprints and are not peer reviewed; others are a thesis and lower-profile journals whose review rigour I cannot assess.
The Brno thesis abstract is in Czech; I relied on my reading of it, and its quantitative results are not visible.

The set has no papers on cryptanalysis of ML-KEM/ML-DSA, quantum hardware timelines, supply-chain or single-vendor dependence, cost, or competing approaches beyond QKD, so those risks are gaps in the evidence and not findings.
The set is dominated by TLS and network-protocol performance, so other areas (firmware signing, HSMs, PKI at scale, embedded devices) are under-covered.
Citation counts are unreliable indicators here (e.g. 153 for a 2025 article in a niche venue).
Only titles, metadata and abstracts were available, so I could not check method details, full results or the exact scope of the papers' claims.
Challenges rely on the evidence set provided. Where I use background knowledge about the standards (for example HQC being a code-based finalist), I flag it as interpretation.
Several evidence entries have future-looking publication dates or are non-peer-reviewed preprints. I have not tried to validate their provenance.
I left S2 and S9 unchallenged: they match the abstracts or are already framed as claims, and the remaining weaknesses were minor.

sources.title: METHODS AND APPARATUS FOR QUANTUM-SAFE SUBSCRIPTION IDENTIFIER PROTECTION [US20260361520A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Devices and methods are disclosed for performing a post-quantum cryptography (PQC)-based subscription identifier protection (SID). In one example, a WTRU may receive subscription permanent identifier (SUPI) privacy protection schemes (SUPIPPSs) from a home network. The WTRU may select a PQC-based SUPIPPS and may use the selected SUPIPPS to encrypt its SUPI to generate a subscription concealed identifier (SUCI). A PQC Signature or a message authentication code (MAC)-Tag may be generated with respect to the SUCI. The WTRU may send the SUCI, the PQC Signature, or the MAC-Tag, and the identifier/name of the selected PQC-based SUPIPPS to the network. Additional embodiments are disclosed.

sources.title: Method and System for Securing Internal API Communications with Dynamic Monitoring and Quantum-Resistant Cryptography [US20260361539A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Systems and methods are disclosed for securing internal API communications through dynamic monitoring and anomaly-driven escalation. A processing system receives an API request with sender and receiver identifiers, headers, and payload, categorizing it as an internal call. Initially, a token-based security module authenticates the call for efficient execution. A monitoring engine analyzes real-time metrics, including call frequency and response consistency, against historical data using machine learning to detect anomalies. Upon anomaly detection, a circuit breaker reroutes the call to a lattice security module, applying quantum-resistant lattice-based cryptography with dynamic parameters to produce a secured call. The circuit breaker logs anomaly details and notifies administrators. The modular system supports alternate post-quantum methods, scales for high-volume traffic, and maintains encrypted audit trails for compliance, ensuring adaptive protection within trusted environments.

sources.title: SYSTEM AND METHODS FOR THREAT-AWARE KEY AND CIPHER ROTATION [US20260359450A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A method and apparatus that implements cryptographic ciphers and key exchange mechanisms, selected from a pool of available ciphers and key mechanisms including but not limited to quantum-resistant ciphers and key mechanisms, which ciphers and keys are in response to the detection, notification, inferential determination, estimation, or prediction of an in-progress, imminent, emerging, and/or anticipated threat.

sources.title: Lattice Secured API Calls with Dual Routing to Ensure Secured APIs for Post Quantum Lattice Construction [US20260361519A1]
sources.abstract: Systems and methods secure API communications against quantum threats using lattice-based cryptography and dual routing. External API calls are automatically routed through a pluggable lattice security module, applying organizational specifications and dynamic parameters to create quantum-resistant encrypted calls. Internal calls use standard security but are monitored in real-time for anomalies, triggering a circuit breaker to reroute through the lattice module if irregularities are detected. A dedicated quantum key distribution channel securely transmits cryptographic basis information to authorized recipients, ensuring external call decryption. The system supports alternate post-quantum methods, customizable lattice rules, and scalable architectures, maintaining performance and interoperability. Dynamic parameter generation ensures unique encryption per call, while continuous monitoring adapts security dynamically, providing robust protection for diverse API ecosystems.

sources.title: Quantum Link Device System and Method for Secure Quantum Authentication and Data Transfer [US20260361419A1]
sources.abstract: A quantum link device system and method for secure quantum authentication and data transfer over 16-17 km. A consumer device, such as a mobile phone or laptop, with an embedded photonic chip (SOI/Si3N4, SNSPDs/APDs) and Qiskit software integrates with quantum hubs generating entangled photons via SPDC (10{circumflex over ( )}8 pairs/s, 95% fidelity). The system enables user authentication via Bell state correlations, device authentication via quantum triangulation (<1 ns latency), and secure data transmission through instant quantum encoding or hybrid CV-DV teleportation. Features include AI anomaly detection (95% accuracy), AES-256 verification, and a control system (10{circumflex over ( )}8 events/s), ensuring 99% breach prevention. Applications include military C2/ISR, healthcare, IoT, finance, and telecommunications, with a hub-and-spoke fiber network supporting scalable, quantum-safe security.

sources.title: Assessing Readiness of Organization for Post-Quantum Cryptography [US20260352575A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Systems and methods are provided for analyzing and defining the readiness or preparedness of a network infrastructure to transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) operation. In one implementation, a method includes a step of collecting information with respect to a current state of a network infrastructure associated with an organization, wherein the collected information is related to compliance of the network infrastructure with PQC standards. The method further includes a step of calculating a PQC readiness score from the collected information. Next, the method includes displaying, on a User Interface (UI), the PQC readiness score and one or more recommended remediation actions for improving the PQC readiness score.

sources.title: System and Method for Quantum-Safe Transaction Security Using Entangled Photons [US20260352453A1]
sources.abstract: A quantum-safe transaction security system and method using entangled photons for authentication in finance, voting, and IoT. Entangled photon pairs are generated and distributed via a scalable fiber and satellite network with quantum repeaters. Entanglement verification, AI-driven anomaly detection, AES-256 redundant verification, and tamper-proof detectors ensure transaction integrity with 95% fidelity over 50 km.

sources.title: QUANTUM-RESISTANT ATTESTED KEY AND MODEL LIFECYCLE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM [US20260352451A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A quantum-resistant system manages the key and model lifecycle of an artificial intelligence model within a trusted execution environment (TEE). A key management engine generates, seals, rotates, and revokes post-quantum keys bound to a hardware-rooted measurement. A secure model update module applies attested changes linking a prior state to a new state. A verifiable fine-tuning module binds, as a single signed unit, digests of training data, gradients, and resulting weights to the measurement. A tamper-evident provenance ledger records the operations and may anchor digests to a public blockchain. The system may mint a self-sovereign agent identity for consumption by a separate orchestration subsystem. Keys, updates, and evidence exist unencrypted only within the TEE and are tamper-evidently bound to the measurement, so an operator cannot alter or suppress them without invalidating the attestation.

METHOD AND SYSTEM FOR STRATEGIZING NETWORK MIGRATION IN ADAPTATION TO POST QUANTUM CRYPTOGRAPHY [EP4835707A1]
sources.abstract: With the advancements in quantum computing, transitioning to quantum-safe cryptography is becoming increasingly critical to keep today's network secure. The present disclosure introduces a method for industrial application network migration. This involves formalizing a Harvest Now Decrypt Later (HNDL) adversarial model, finding a risk score of a successful HNDL attack in any network links followed by in any network component. Graph theory and the Markov chain is used for finding out the central network points. The centrality of network points is measured using a centrality score. The central points are the points in the network, compromising those can compromise a significant part of the total network. Finally, a critical score is given to network points based on risk score, centrality score and metadata about the network points. This critical score can be a priority number given to the network points to rank them for migration to quantum safe state.

sources.title: SEED CACHING TO OVERCOME PQC STORAGE BOTTLENECKS [US20260342559A1]
sources.abstract: Devices, systems, and methods for memory-efficient post-quantum (PQ) cryptography are provided. A method includes generating, by a hardware security module (HSM), a cryptographic seed, storing, by the HSM, the cryptographic seed, receiving, by the HSM and from a cryptographic processor, a request for the cryptographic seed, and responsive to the request, providing, by the HSM and to the cryptographic processor, the cryptographic seed.

sources.title: SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR QUANTUM-RESISTANT CRYPTOGRAPHIC REFLECTION ARCHITECTURE FOR DISTRIBUTED-LEDGER TRANSACTION DATA [US20260342601A1]
sources.abstract: A computer-implemented system for quantum-resistant cryptographic protection of distributed-ledger transaction data. Upon close of a transaction block, a reflection generation engine generates N cryptographic reflections, each comprising a multi-component commitment including content, state, temporal, chain anchor, sibling reflection, and algorithm fingerprint components. Reflections are constructed using a heterogeneous set of cryptographic primitives such that no two reflections share identical primitives, and reflections do not contain recoverable transaction data. Each reflection is distributed to a corresponding vault implemented as a cloud storage service, a custodial storage arrangement, a sovereign data facility, or a smart contract repository, each vault operating under a distinct custody and jurisdictional regime. An anomaly-aware multi-factor authentication gate validates retrieval requests. A three-tier verification module supports existence proof, integrity attestation, and forensic recovery modes.

sources.title: POST-QUANTUM CRYPTOGRAPHY USING HIGH-MEMORY MASKED CONVOLUTIONAL CODES WITH DUAL-LAYER ERROR MECHANISMS [WO2026224702A1]
sources.abstract: A cryptographic encryption system for securing communications resistant to quantum computing attacks. The sender processes a plaintext vector by computing a remainder polynomial and appending its coefficients to form an augmented vector, multiplies the augmented vector by a public key derived from a masked convolutional code, and introduces random errors into the resulting ciphertext sufficient to increase cryptanalytic resistance while maintaining decodability, thereby generating an error-injected ciphertext. The recipient recovers the plaintext by applying an inverse permutation to the error-injected ciphertext, generating candidate unmasked vectors by subtracting possible masking vectors, performing polynomial division on constituent polynomials of each candidate to form candidate decoded vectors, applying parallel Viterbi decoding to identify the most likely codeword, transforming the codeword using an inverse transformation matrix, verifying the result using a predetermined error detection polynomial, and extracting the plaintext vector.

sources.title: ACCEPTANCE-CONTROL LAYER FOR VERIFIED AI-GENERATED CODE [US20260339818A1]
sources.abstract: Disclosed is an acceptance-control layer for AI-generated software code, implemented as a system, method, and non-transitory computer-readable medium. A hardware-enforced deployment gate prevents transmission of candidate code outside a trusted execution environment (TEE) until four conditions are simultaneously satisfied: (i) a formal verification engine produces a machine-checkable proof of one or more correctness properties of the candidate code; (ii) a quantum-resistant cryptographic module produces attestation evidence binding the candidate code, the AI agents, and the proof to the hardware-rooted TEE measurement using one or more post-quantum cryptographic algorithms; (iii) a hardware-rooted consensus engine satisfies a policy-defined threshold among a plurality of validators whose eligibility is bound to the hardware-rooted measurement; and (iv) the candidate code, the proof, the attestation evidence, and the consensus decision are recorded in a tamper-evident provenance ledger supporting independent third-party verification.

sources.title: STABLECOIN ECOSYSTEM WITH MULTI-ASSET COLLATERAL, AI-GOVERNED MONETARY POLICY, POST-QUANTUM CRYPTOGRAPHY, AND INTEGRATED UGC LICENSING [WO2026222126A1]
sources.abstract: The present invention pertains to a blockchain-based stablecoin ecosystem integrating Al-driven monetary policy, algorithmically managed multi-asset reserves, tranche-segmented liquidity, decentralized oracle- verified proof-of-reserve, Al-augmented governance, NTT-based licensing with stablecoin royalty micropayments, a threshold-signature cross-chain lock-and-mint bridge, a user-centric wallet payment-rails interface, a content creator-economy SDK, and a crypto-agile quantum-resistant security framework. The modules cooperate to maintain price stability, ensure transparent and fully backed cross-chain circulation, enable creator monetization, facilitate mainstream payment integration, and provide consumer loyalty rewards, thereby addressing known shortcomings of existing single-asset or algorithmic stablecoins on Ethereum and other blockchain networks while extending the stablecoin's utility into everyday commerce.

sources.title: Digital Identity and Consent Management System [US20260330450A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A digital identity and consent management standard (DICMS), providing a unified, scalable framework for user-driven consent across decentralized, AI, web3 and web4 ecosystems. Leveraging a decentralized infrastructure, cryptographic network protocols, and integrates deferred cryptographic proofs and quantum-resistant encryption to redefine consent validation. This technology disclosed herein introduces a Dynamic Data Transformation Layer (DDTL) that anonymizes and provisions compliant first-party user data for enterprise applications while ensuring secure, ethical data usage. Supporting interoperability across digital spectrums, the framework aligns with global compliance standards like GDPR and CCPA and prepares for future technologies, including Web4 ecosystems and large language models (LLMs). The technology disclosed herein introduces a proof-of-humanity (POH) option under a decentralized autonomous organization (DAO) consent standard, allowing secure user opt-ins for KYC identity claims, data sovereignty, and resource delivery across public and private services.

A method includes authenticating, by a device and with a first server, using a legacy device identity, receiving and installing, by the device, a firmware upgrade that provides the device an ability to communicate in a PQS manner, establishing a PQS communication channel between the device and a second server, mutually authenticating, by the device and with the second server, using a PQ identity (PQI) of the device, the PQI different from the legacy identity, and responsive to successful mutual authentication, communicating between the device and the second server, using the PQS communication channel.

sources.title: Data processing system [GB2706015A]
sources.abstract: A data processing system is disclosed, comprising first 102 and second non-volatile storage circuitry 108 and processing circuitry; the first non-volatile storage 102 stores a cryptographic software digest 104, while the second non-volatile storage stores first program code for cryptographic software 110 and second program code for application software 112; processing circuitry coupled to both storage circuits executes boot logic 106 to compute a hash value 202 of the cryptographic software and compare it 206 with the digest; if the hash value conforms to the digest, the processing circuitry executes the first program code to implement the cryptographic software 208, which includes a cryptographic verification algorithm 212 to verify the second program code, the application software; based on the outcome the second program code is executed 214. This system enables crypto agility wherein multiple cryptographic algorithms can be stored in a bootloader without consuming additional non-volatile memory (NVRAM). Thus, sophisticated algorithms for secure boot can be implemented in the cryptographic software including RSA, ECDSA, PQC, CRYSTALS-Kyber (ML-KEM), SPHINCS (SLH-DSA), Extended Merkle Signature Scheme (XMSS). The digest may be written to a one-time programmable (OTP) memory which may also store a digital signature. [Fig. 2]

sources.title: QUANTUM SAFE EMAIL ENCRYPTION SYSTEM AND METHOD [EP4822572A1]
sources.abstract: Quantum safe email encryption system and method, according to the invention, use quantum computing for device registration, authentication, and encryption key management. This invention leverages Quantum Random Number Generators (QRNGs) and Quantum Computing Algorithms to ensure post-quantum security, preventing unauthorized access to encrypted email communications.

sources.title: QUANTUM RESISTANT TRUST ORCHESTRATION FOR BRAIN COMPUTER INTERFACES [US20260310787A1]
sources.abstract: A quantum-resistant trust orchestration system for brain-computer interfaces assigns trust-weighted authority to neural interpretations, correlates outcomes to neural intent, and enables automated rollback. The system generates immutable governance records suitable for medical, regulatory, and cross-domain deployment of brain-computer interface systems.

sources.title: Dynamic Multi-Axis Cubit Array (DMAQA) for AI-Optimized Quantum Tensor Computation [CA3268010A1]
sources.abstract: The Dynamic Multi-Axis Qubit Array (DMAQA) is an AI-driven quantum tensor processing system designed to optimize quantum state evolution, tensor network operations, and AIaccelerated computations. DMAQA integrates multi-axis qubit control, deep reinforcement learning for workload balancing, and hybrid quantum-classical execution, making it highly applicable to quantum simulations, AI model training, cryptographic security, and blockchain verification. Key Features: • Multi-Axis Qubit Array for Tensor Evolution – Optimized processing of high-dimensional quantum states for AI-driven computations. • AI-Assisted Workload Balancing – Uses reinforcement learning to dynamically predict and allocate quantum-classical compute resources. • Hybrid Quantum-Classical Execution – Seamlessly distributes tasks across QPUs, GPUs, CPUs, and TPUs, reducing latency and improving performance. • Scalability Beyond 1024 Qubits – Enables large-scale quantum tensor computations, surpassing current 512-qubit limitations. • Post-Quantum Cryptographic Security – Implements SHA-3 hashing, Kyber key exchange, and Dilithium signatures to ensure quantum-resistant blockchain verification. DMAQA improves tensor contractions, minimizes processing bottlenecks, and enables AI-assisted workload redistribution, ensuring high-speed, secure, and energy-efficient quantum-AI computing.

draft.summary: Research and patent activity on post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is accelerating sharply. Papers rose from 849 in 2024 to 1,926 in 2025, and 2,979 papers by 20 Oct 2026 compare with 1,352 a year earlier. Patent publications show the same pattern (349 vs 159 year to date), so momentum is still building. Standards exist (FIPS 203/204/205), and early evidence of commercial offerings and migration planning comes from a telecom (M2), a bank (M3), Cisco's risk disclosure (M1) and patents (P1-P5). The evidence for paying customers, PQC revenue and volume deployment is thin. Several deployment claims come from unverified social posts (X2, X3), and some filings are from micro-cap companies with no shown PQC product. Performance evidence conflicts (R3, C2), and the urgency rests on an unexamined assumption about when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer will arrive (R8, C5). Research activity is not commercial success, and the main uncertainty is how fast migration spending turns into revenue, and for whom.
draft.plain_summary: Post-quantum cryptography means new ways of locking data so that future powerful quantum computers cannot break the locks. Research, patents and early company activity are growing fast, and official standards now exist. The main thing that could slow it down is that nobody knows when such quantum computers will arrive, and switching old systems over is slow, costly and complicated.

Social posts on US/UK discovery mandates are unverified (X1). No findings show revenue, contract values or customer counts.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: If the 2030 compliance deadline cited by one micro-cap filer (M4) and the reported discovery mandates (X1) hold, migration work could grow. The evidence suggests the bottleneck is operational (inventory, configuration, legacy protocols) rather than algorithmic (R6, M3). Overhead from larger handshakes and hybrid profiles may slow rollout (R1, C4), and performance results conflict (R3).

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: The evidence does not say when quantum computers capable of breaking current cryptography will exist (R8, C5), so long-run demand rests on an assumed threat timeline. Security of the new schemes is conjectured, not proven (R4), and the standard set may diversify (C1), so the design mix could change.

bull.label: forecast
bull.narrative: Compliance deadlines and government discovery mandates force regulated sectors to migrate. Standardised algorithms perform acceptably (S3), and telecom and security vendors turn PQC into paid services (M2, X3), supported by rising patent filings on migration and API security (P1, P5).

base.label: forecast
base.narrative: Migration proceeds slowly and unevenly, led by large regulated organisations and vendors who treat it first as a risk and compliance cost (M8). Commercial offerings grow gradually in telecom and security services. Research and patent activity stays high, but revenue attribution stays hard to see.

bear.label: forecast
bear.narrative: Operational friction, handshake and bandwidth overhead (R1), denial-of-service exposure (R2), side-channel issues (R5) and an unclear quantum timeline (R8) delay spending. A cryptanalytic weakness in a standardised scheme (R4) would force rework. Most small filers mentioning PQC (M5, M6, M7) never show a real product.
